data.title: Trump nominates Wesley Hunt to Saudi Arabia ambassador post
data.description:
President Trump on Monday nominated Rep. Wesley Hunt (R-Texas) to serve as U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia.

Trump sent the nominations of Hunt and a slew of other individuals to the Senate, which has to confirm his appointments.

The U.S. has not had a full-time ambassador to Saudi Arabia since Michael Ratney left office at the end of the Biden administration. Jennifer Larson, a career member of the State Department’s Foreign Service, has led the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh on an interim basis since mid-August — succeeding Alison Dilworth.

Hunt is departing the lower chamber after two terms representing Texas’s 38th Congressional District. The 44-year-old former Army officer finished third in the Lone Star State’s Senate GOP primary in March, a race state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) won via runoff over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

The Texas representative is set to leave the House at the end of his term in January. In a statement, Hunt said it was the “honor of a lifetime” for Trump to nominate him to the ambassadorship post.

“Having served in the region both in combat as an Army officer and for two years as a diplomatic liaison in the Kingdom, I understand the strategic importance of the partnership between the United States and Saudi Arabia and the profound responsibility of this position,” Hunt said.

“When confirmed, I will serve with humility and honor, advance his vision of peace through strength and deepen this vital partnership,” he added.

The Hill has reached out to a Hunt spokesperson regarding whether the GOP lawmaker will resign from the House, if confirmed.

Trump and his family have business ties to Saudi Arabia, and the president has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman — whom U.S. intelligence said “approved” the 2018 operation that resulted in the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi.

Last month, the Trump administration sent a nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia to Congress. Under the 30-year deal, U.S. companies would be able to develop the kingdom’s civil nuclear infrastructure.

The president has stipulated, though, that Saudi Arabia must normalize ties with Israel for the deal to take effect.

data.title: Trump guts climate rules for coal and gas power plants
data.description:
The Trump administration on Monday gutted regulations that limited planet-warming emissions from coal- and gas-fired power plants. 

The move allows a sector that makes up a large share of the U.S.’s climate change contributions to release greenhouse gases unchecked by the government. It’s expected to be a win for the fossil fuel industry, while allowing the release of significantly more planet-heating pollution.

When it proposed to kill the regulations entirely last year, the Trump administration estimated that in the year 2035 alone, this would result in the release of 123 million more metric tons of carbon dioxide, equivalent to putting an additional 28.7 million gas-powered cars on the road.

Monday’s move could be slightly different. While it is expected to repeal large swaths of Biden-era power plant regulations, Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) assistant administrator Aaron Szabo told reporters that limited pieces of Biden- and Obama-era regs would remain in place. 

In addition to Monday’s final rule, the EPA proposed to find that the Clean Air Act does not give it the authority to regulate power plant emissions due to their climate impacts. If finalized, Szabo said that this move could block future administrations from regulating power plants’ climate emissions. 

Overall, he said that the moves would allow “American families and businesses experience lower electricity costs … thanks to an increased power supply.”

The moves come as high electricity demand and increasing power prices continue to be a major political issue. Last year’s analysis found that in 2035, axing power plant climate rules could reduce electricity prices by an average of 1.4 percent.

In a press release, the EPA said that it expects its final rule to save $310 billion.

President Trump has falsely said that climate change is a “hoax” on multiple occasions, and his administration has broadly sought to cut back or eliminate climate regulations. It recently repealed all climate rules for cars and trucks, saying their emissions did not pose a threat to the public.

Climate change has been linked to worsening heat waves and extreme weather. The U.S. power sector is a major driver of planet-warming emissions, responsible for a quarter of total U.S. emissions. 

Environmental activists recoiled at the Trump administration’s latest rollback before news of it was officially announced.

“It’s really just the Trump EPA putting their head in the sand,” said Meredith Hankins, federal climate legal director at the Natural Resources Defense Council. “I mean, you can look at the weather we experienced this summer, the heat waves on the Fourth of July. We’re going into an El Niño season with potential hurricanes and even more extreme weather. We see the impacts of climate change all around us every day, and the Trump EPA is trying to say, ‘Well, that’s not our problem.'”

Meanwhile, industry players celebrated the move.

Rachael Marsh, chief legal officer at the Edison Electric Institute, a trade group representing power companies, said in a statement that it “welcomes EPA’s repeal” of the Biden-era rule. 

The EPA’s action repeals most of a Biden-era rule that would have required existing coal plants and new gas plants to prevent 90 percent of their carbon dioxide emissions from entering the atmosphere.

data.title: Jeffries calls on Congress to stay in Washington to address AI concerns
data.description:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is calling on House GOP leaders to remain in Washington to allow Congress to consider new limits on AI companies following dire warnings from industry insiders about the threat the technology poses to humanity. 

Speaking to reporters Monday in the Capitol, Jeffries said the calls for a slowdown from within the industry should be a wakeup call for lawmakers in the Capitol, who have dabbled at the edges of AI regulation for years without taking any significant steps to ensure public safety.

Jeffries did not promote specific reforms, but urged Congress to delay its long, pre-election recess “until something is done decisively to protect the safety and the well-being of the American people.”

“Republicans have completely abandoned their responsibility to legislate and engage in public policy efforts in a responsible fashion in the area of artificial intelligence,” Jeffries said.

The pressure is unlikely to bear fruit. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) opposes any swift action on new AI regulations, warning that hasty new limits risk overburdening American technology companies to the benefit of America’s global adversaries. 

“The reflex of legislative bodies is to cover things up with red tape and in hyperregulation,” Johnson told reporters Monday in the Capitol. “If you do that, then you lose your edge.”

Johnson has scheduled the House to adjourn on Thursday and remain in recess through the Nov. 3 elections.

Still, the public anxieties surrounding AI — and the related issue of data centers, which are helping to fuel the AI boom — have increasingly become campaign fodder heading into the midterms, when both the House and Senate are up for grabs. 

The issue reached new heights over the weekend when three top leaders in the AI industry — Dario Amodei, Elon Musk and Sam Altman — urged a more cautious approach to the development of the technology. A failure to do so, Amodei, the head of Anthropic, warned in a long blog post, could lead to global catastrophe. 

President Trump has come out strongly in favor of data centers and against regulating AI — two positions that put him at odds with the majority of voters. And Democrats are highlighting both topics to portray the president and other GOP leaders as out of touch with public sentiment heading to the polls. 

“They’re not really concerned about over-regulation. They want no regulation,” Jeffries said. “And that’s the height of irresponsibility.” 

Jeffries noted that, in the previous Congress, he and former Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.) had launched an AI task force designed to balance the success of American AI companies with public safety precautions. The panel did not survive the transition into the new Congress — a development Jeffries blamed on Trump’s return to the White House.

“Republicans in this Congress, at the direction of Donald Trump, detonated that bipartisan effort and endangered the health and the safety and the well-being of the American people in doing so,” he said.

data.title: Macklemore says Robert Kraft, stadium owners fueled his ouster from Ed Sheeran's tour over call to 'free Palestine'
data.description:
Rapper Macklemore said Monday that stadium owners, among them Robert Kraft of the New England Patriots, fueled his ouster from pop star Ed Sheeran’s ongoing tour following his pro-Palestinian advocacy.

In a post on Instagram, the Seattle rapper said that Sheeran “and his team have made the decision to remove me from The Loop tour.”

Per The Hollywood Reporter, pro-Israel groups went after Macklemore earlier this month after he offered up a “free Palestine” message in an opening set for Sheeran at MetLife Stadium on Sept. 4. Pink, another key figure of the early 2010s pop scene, responded to Macklemore’s message and faced pushback for elevating an effort to get the rapper axed from the tour, according to the outlet.

“Last Monday, in the middle of all the media attention surrounding Pink and what I said at MetLife, Ed told me that Robert Kraft called him. We were scheduled to play Gillette Stadium later this month, which is owned by the Kraft Group,” Macklemore wrote in his Monday Instagram post.

“Ed told me that Kraft said I would not be allowed to perform in his stadium. Ed also told me that Kraft had rallied some of the other stadium owners and collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues,” he added.

Macklemore added later in his lengthy Instagram post that if the words “free Palestine” got him kicked off the stage, “while turning the conversation back to Palestine, than it was the most successful tour I’ve ever been on.”

Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza, which began close to three years ago, has led to the deaths of tens of thousands of Palestinians, caused mass destruction of infrastructure in the territory and sparked a humanitarian crisis. A number of humanitarian and human rights groups have accused Israel of committing a “genocide” in the territory.

Macklemore has previously been accused of antisemitic actions. In spring 2014, the rapper issued an apology over a costume he wore while performing that critics labeled as antisemitic, according to the BBC.

The Hill has reached out to the Kraft Group, a representative for Sheeran and Messina Touring Group for comment.

data.title: Trump adds extra sanctions to Russian bank for ties to Iran
data.description:
The Trump administration on Monday added extra sanctions on one of Russia’s largest financial institutions, VTB, over its ties to Iran, layering on penalties first imposed because of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. 

The Treasury Department is redesignating VTB as part of the administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast.” The sanctions campaign was launched in August to squeeze Iran financially as the Islamic Republic has resisted more than six months of U.S. military bombardment and effectively held the world’s energy supply hostage through its military threats on the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s support for the Houthis in Yemen, who have recently taken over critical infrastructure on the Red Sea, has recently threatened another key energy maritime route.

“Under Operation Economic Outcast, Treasury will continue to target and disrupt those who provide material, technological, or financial support that allows the Iranian regime to sustain its terrorist enterprise,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent.

“Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran’s enablers.”

VTB is Russia’s second largest financial institution with thousands of branches across the world, particularly across India, southeast Asia and China. The Biden administration first designated the bank in 2022 following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. 

The Trump administration’s new sanctions are an effort to encourage countries and institutions to cut ties with VTB by publicizing its role helping Iran evade sanctions and finance its international terrorism activity. 

This includes VTB helping Iran move billions of dollars in frozen assets and enabling tens of millions of dollars in transactions for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Force (IRGC), the military force primarily responsible for Iran’s terrorist activity across the world.   

State Department spokesperson Tommy Piggott said today’s actions “sends a clear message to governments and financial institutions considering similar arrangements: any effort to help Iran evade sanctions will carry serious consequences, including exposure to U.S. financial restrictions.”

Still, it’s not entirely clear the main impact of the additional sanctions. Treasury officials will meet with international financial institutions this week to provide them information to shut down revenue streams and procurement networks tied to the Iranian regime, the IRGC, Iran’s terrorist proxies and other beneficiaries, The Hill has learned. 

The sanctions prevent any U.S. person or entity from doing business with VTB and prohibits transactions with any entities with a 50 percent or more ownership by the blocked entity.

data.title: Mahmoud Khalil sues Columbia, accusing it of 'indifference' to harassment of pro-Palestinian protesters
data.description:
Mahmoud Khalil, a prominent pro-Palestinian demonstrator targeted by the Trump administration, and other former Columbia University student activists are suing their alma mater over its alleged indifference to harassment they faced there.  

The lawsuit filed Monday alleges Columbia violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act when dealing with incidents against the Palestine Working Group (PWG), an organization the university suspended indefinitely in May 2025.  

Khalil, who previously led the student group, was the first in a concerted campaign by the Trump administration to attempt to deport pro-Palestinian foreign students. He was arrested in March 2025 and held in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody for months. 

Khalil is still fighting the Trump administration’s deportation efforts and has taken his appeals to the Supreme Court after a circuit court ruled a federal judge did not have the ability to bar the Trump administration from deporting him.  

The lawsuit is looking to force Columbia to reinstate PWG, take greater action against anti-Muslin discrimination, allow Khalil back on campus and pay monetary damages. 

“Columbia laid the groundwork for my targeting by the Trump administration through its deliberate indifference and discrimination against Palestinian students,” Khalil said in a statement. “For over two years, we pleaded with Columbia, and Columbia did not care. Our safety and wellbeing did not serve the ideological project its Board of Trustees was protecting, so they traded us away. We are suing because no one should go through the hell Columbia put us through.” 

The lawsuit alleges members of PWG were “antagonized and harassed without consequence” since its creation in 2018, but that the harassment accelerated following Oct. 7, 2023, after Hamas attacked Israel.  

It said the harassment included doxxing of members by outside groups, threats against its members by peers on campus and Columbia itself calling the organization a “hostile group.” 

Reached for comment, a spokesperson for Columbia declined to respond directly to the lawsuit, but said that “Creating a campus environment where every member of our community feels welcome, supported, and safe is fundamental to who we are as a University. It is also a responsibility we take seriously.

“Columbia is committed to protecting our community from discrimination and harassment, and responding promptly and appropriately when concerns arise,” the spokesperson said.  

Columbia was at the center of the pro-Palestinian student protests that spread like wildfire across the country in the spring of 2024, leading to thousands of arrests on campuses. The university later paid an over $200 million fine to the Trump administration for the pro-Palestinian encampment on campus and agreed to change disciplinary and other school policies.

data.title: Chicago Democratic mayor says he'll run for reelection
data.description:
Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson (D) announced Sunday he is running for reelection, more than three years after he ascended to the office.

“My name is Brandon Johnson, and I am running for reelection in the greatest fricking city in the world, Chicago,” an impassioned Johnson said at a rally, to cheers of “four more years” from attendees.

Johnson, formerly on the Cook County Board of Commissioners, outlasted a crowded field, which included then-Mayor Lori Lightfoot (D), in the nonpartisan mayoral race in 2023.

Voters in the Windy City will head to the polls in February, with a runoff in April if no candidate receives majority support.

The first-term mayor, a staunch progressive, touted his work as mayor on Sunday. The 50-year-old said his “North Star” is working for “the many, and not the few.”

Johnson added, “Real transformation has never come from the top down but from the bottom up.”

Salaries for private industry workers increased by 3.9 percent in the Chicago metro area in June, ahead of the national average of 3.3 percent, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Reports of certain violent crimes have also decreased during Johnson’s tenure. The murder rate, up slightly from last year, is down 33 percent from 2023, according to data from the Chicago Police Department (CPD).

Sexual assaults, robberies and burglaries are down by 10 percent, 53 percent and 25 percent relative to 2023, respectively, while thefts are up by 3 percent, per the CPD data.

But earlier this year, Fitch Ratings downgraded Chicago’s credit rating after Johnson and the city council battled until the 11th hour over a spending plan last December. The impasse stemmed from Johnson’s preference to reinstitute the employer head tax.

Last year, Johnson battled with the Trump administration over its surge of federal immigration officers to Chicago. A recent study from the University of Illinois Chicago’s Great Cities Institute found that the roughly two-month operation cost local businesses more than $1.2 billion last year.

Johnson will have to beat multiple challengers to clinch a second term. Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias (D), Illinois State Comptroller Susana Mendoza (D) and Rep. Mike Quigley (D-Ill.) are among a crowded group vying for Johnson’s office.

data.title: Oil prices up after new strikes on Saudi infrastructure
data.description:
Oil prices on Monday leaped more than 4 percent after Yemen-based militant Houthis struck Saudi Arabia’s infrastructure and ships, leaving one crucial pipeline out of service for weeks.

The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent crude, settled at $105.66 per barrel as of Monday afternoon. West Texas Intermediate (WTI), the benchmark in the U.S., rose to $101.28.

The average price of gas in the U.S. reached $4.32, a 7-cent increase since last week, and the average price for diesel reached $6.23, a new record, both according to data from AAA.

Saudi Arabia’s 745-mile-long East-West Pipeline has helped the government move crude production from the Persian Gulf ports to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, where tankers can export oil.

Saudi officials familiar with the Thursday attack on the pipeline told the Associated Press that it could take 3-5 weeks to repair, though it could partially work while crews work to fix it. The pipeline moved a weekly average of 2.6 million to 4 million barrels a day since late August.

The Norway-based energy analyst Rystad Energy said Monday that the increase in the price of Brent crude “is a clear signal that the market is increasingly pricing in a significant loss of supply.”

The Houthis, a proxy of the Iranian regime, entered the U.S.-Israeli conflict in Iran to retaliate against Gulf state attacks on Iran after calling on Persian Gulf countries, the U.S. and Israel to seek a path to diplomacy and peace with Iran. They warned that they would retaliate if the conflict escalated.

The Houthis also captured the crucial islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish, which are both located 100 miles north of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to Saudi Arabia’s key Asian markets. The islands are also 20 miles from a U.S. military base in Djibouti in the Horn of Africa.

The rebels also took over the port city of Mokha, another Red Sea port crucial to shipping, risking opening up a new front in the Iran war. The Saudis have reportedly urged President Trump to launch strikes on the Houthis, while the U.S. has sent more than 100 advisors to help the Saudis in their fight with the rebel forces.

Oil exports through the Red Sea after passing through the East-West Pipeline have been an alternative to exporting oil out of the Strait of Hormuz. The Iranian regime has effectively cut off the transit of oil out of the region in response to U.S. strikes, causing gas and oil prices to skyrocket.

Diesel prices have soared to record highs as Ukraine carries out its drone strikes on Russian refineries. Trump urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to call off further attacks on these refineries.

“He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters on Sunday. We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”

data.title: Thune: Legislation to regulate AI needs to have a 'light touch'
data.description:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) on Monday said any legislation Congress passes to regulate AI must have a “light touch” so as not to stifle innovation and tempered recent warnings that superintelligent AI could exterminate humanity as a “worst-case scenario.”

“It needs to strike a balance, light touch. You don’t want to stifle innovation but you also want to make sure that the more advanced threats can be mitigated,” he told reporters.

“Obviously there’s a responsibility for the companies to do that when it comes to the frontier on some of these models,” he added. “There is a way in which Congress can put guardrails around those types of more consequential threats without in any way harming our ability to stay ahead in the AI race, which I also think is very important.”

Thune made his comments after Jacob Coxon, a former researcher for OpenAI and Anthropic, warned that neither company is acting responsibility and are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

This has fueled fears that superintelligent AI could turn against humanity with devastating consequences, something that Thune on Monday downplayed as a “worst-case scenario.”

“I think there are some of these frontier models … I think there are some potential consequential risks associated with AI. But there are always people who are creating a worst-case-scenario-type conversation out there and I think that you have to try, like all things, figure out what the realistic approach ought to be,” he said.

“Put guardrails around it, like I said, I think on some of these advanced-risk-type models some guardrails there make sense to me but I think you want to do it in a light-touch way that doesn’t squash innovation,” he added. “We are in a race with China and I think there’s huge upside, obviously, with AI as well. There are a lot of benefits to society along with some risks.”

Thune spoke to reporters after Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) called on the Trump administration to provide a classified briefing to all senators on the risks posed by AI.

“Warning bells are ringing louder than they ever have – and the Trump administration is looking the other way. Well, if they won’t hold themselves accountable, we will. And if Trump does not act, Congress must,” Schumer said in a statement Monday morning.

He said officials need to answer questions about three areas of concern related to AI.

He wants the administration to provide a full accounting of its new framework for testing the most powerful frontier AI models and to detail what it’s doing to prevent AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment from flowing to China.

Schumer said it also needs to explain its plans to defend the United States from increasingly sophisticated AI-enabled cyberattacks.

Trump, meanwhile, has downplayed the dangers and pushed back on calls for more guardrails around AI.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” he wrote on Truth Social. “The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’” he wrote on Truth Social Monday. “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!” There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”

data.title: Sanders, Bannon to speak at event calling for AI controls
data.description:
Political figures across the aisle, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and former Trump White House adviser Steve Bannon, are finding themselves on the same side of a growing fight over artificial intelligence regulations.

Sanders and Bannon are among a handful of political leaders speaking Tuesday at an event advocating controls to keep humans in charge of AI.

The “Pro-Human Assembly,, hosted by the nonprofit Future of Life Institute in D.C., comes as Washington scrambles to address the risks and safety concerns growing around AI.

Concerns were supercharged last week after AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and claimed in an X post that researchers at the frontier labs “believe AI could kill all humans” but push forward anyway.

Coxon warned superintelligence — a hypothetical AI agent that outperforms all of humanity’s cognitive performance — could destroy all of humanity if the technology’s development does not slow down.

Sanders is one of the loudest voices on the left calling for AI regulations. He and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) called for a permanent ban on the development and deployment of superintelligence in the wake of recent hackings involving “rogue” models.

Bannon has taken a populist approach to AI, repeatedly warning over the risks of AI and data centers used to power the technology’s development.

Other speakers include Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), along with Casar, Reps. Chip Roy (R-Texas), Lori Trahan (D-Mass.), Don Beyer (D-Va.) and New York State Assemblyman Alex Bores, who ran a congressional campaign advocating for better oversight of AI model development.

While Democrats and Republicans remain far apart on how to regulate the technology, a growing number of lawmakers agree more needs to be done to ensure AI is developed safely, with the country’s labor workforce in mind.

President Trump, an ally of Bannon, is doubling down on his support for the AI and data center industry. He argued in a post on Truth Social on Monday “only protections needed are a “strong and smart (High IQ!) President,” claiming the government has tremendous criminal and regulatory power” over AI firms already.
